title: Putin is far from isolated. Europe must play him at the long game
gist: Chatham House argues Putin's escalating diplomacy and battlefield aggression reflect confidence, not desperation, because Russia's partnerships with China, India and Kazakhstan give it enough economic integration and diplomatic legitimacy to absorb Western pressure; the author urges Europe to abandon its 'choose a side' strategy toward the Global South and instead compete for influence patiently over the long term.

insights.claim: In a Moscow meeting on 5 September 2026 lasting more than three hours, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed ending the war with Putin, but the Kremlin gave no indication it would relax its core demands of Ukrainian territorial concessions and restrictions on Kyiv's future security alignment.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: A near-term negotiated settlement remains unlikely; scenarios pricing a quick end to the war should be discounted.
insights.quote: gave no indication that it was ready to relax its demands: Ukrainian territorial concessions and restrictions on Kyiv’s future security alignment.
insights.locator: No backing down

insights.claim: Putin rebuffed an offer from Volodymyr Zelenskyy to meet him at the G20 summit in Miami in December 2026, and Russian attacks intensified in the days that followed.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: Kremlin shows no urgency to engage even at high-visibility diplomatic venues, reinforcing a protracted-conflict base case.
insights.quote: an offer by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to meet Putin at December’s G20 summit in Miami was rebuffed.
insights.locator: No backing down

insights.claim: On 13 September 2026 a Russian drone struck railway infrastructure near Yahodyn shortly after a train carrying Boris Johnson and former CIA director David Petraeus had passed through, as part of Russia's largest drone barrage in months targeting Ukrainian transport, energy and civilian infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: Escalation is reaching close to Western officials and transport corridors, raising the risk premium on Ukraine-adjacent logistics and infrastructure.
insights.quote: the strike was part of Russia’s largest drone barrage in months and followed intensified attacks on Ukrainian transport, energy and civilian infrastructure.
insights.locator: On 13 September, a Russian drone struck

insights.claim: The common European reading that Russia's intensified attacks signal desperation is a miscalculation; the combination of diplomatic impassivity and calibrated escalation is a deliberate strategy that may be stronger than it appears.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: Investors and policymakers should not treat Russian escalation as a leading indicator of imminent capitulation or a near-term deal.
insights.quote: the Kremlin’s strategy of blended diplomatic impassivity and calibrated escalation may be stronger than it looks.
insights.locator: No backing down

insights.claim: Despite extraordinary Russian losses, slow and costly territorial advances, and Ukrainian gains in several sectors, Putin behaves as though time is on his side and he retains room for manoeuvre.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: War-duration risk should be assessed by Putin's external partnerships and confidence, not purely by battlefield attrition metrics.
insights.quote: Putin behaves like someone who still believes time is on his side and that he retains room for manoeuvre.
insights.locator: Yet the conclusion that Russian escalation

insights.claim: Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev publicly said in July 2026, sitting alongside Putin in Omsk, that the Ukraine conflict should be frozen and negotiations resumed, but the Kremlin promptly rejected the idea of a freeze.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: Even friendly interlocutors' peace overtures carry no real leverage over Kremlin decision-making.
insights.quote: Sitting alongside Putin in Omsk, Tokayev said the conflict should be frozen and negotiations resumed.
insights.locator: Putin can (still) afford to ignore friendly advice

insights.claim: Indian PM Narendra Modi told Putin at the SCO summit in Bishkek on 31 August 2026 that the world needed to move 'from endless war to end of war,' yet less than two weeks later at the BRICS summit discussed a bilateral trade target of $100 billion with Putin.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: India's rhetorical criticism of the war coexists with deepening economic commitment to Russia; expect trade ties to keep expanding regardless of diplomatic messaging.
insights.quote: less than two weeks later, during the BRICS summit, discussed a bilateral trade target of $100 billion with Putin.
insights.locator: Narendra Modi went a step further

insights.claim: Governments such as India and Kazakhstan genuinely want the Ukraine war to end, but that does not mean they are willing to make their relations with Russia conditional on it, which underpins Putin's confidence.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: Do not expect Global South governments' war-end rhetoric to translate into sanctions or reduced trade with Russia.
insights.quote: that does not mean they are prepared to make their relations with Russia conditional upon it.
insights.locator: There is no reason to doubt

insights.claim: The New Delhi BRICS declaration criticised unilateral sanctions and trade restrictions while avoiding directly confronting Russia over Ukraine, and these sustained Asian partnerships give Moscow economic integration, diplomatic legitimacy and a respected role in international groupings that it needs almost as much as battlefield support.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: BRICS bloc consensus continues to shield Russia from coordinated multilateral criticism, reducing the odds of bloc-wide pressure or isolation.
insights.quote: the New Delhi BRICS declaration criticised unilateral sanctions and trade restrictions while avoiding directly confronting Russia over Ukraine.
insights.locator: Meanwhile the New Delhi BRICS declaration

insights.claim: China's economy is roughly eight times larger than Russia's, and Russia conducts at least 34 per cent of its international trade with China while Russia accounts for only about 4 per cent of China's trade, a real asymmetry that underlies Europe's 'vassal' framing of Russia.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: Quantifies Russia's trade dependency on China, a key metric for assessing Russia's economic exposure to a single partner.
insights.quote: China’s economy is roughly eight times larger than Russia’s. And Russia conducts at least 34 per cent of its international trade with China, whereas Russia accounts for only around 4 per cent of China’s.
insights.locator: Russia is valuable to China too

insights.claim: The 'vassal' framing misses that Beijing has strategic reasons to keep Moscow strong enough to remain an independent power, given Russia's nuclear arsenal, permanent UN Security Council seat, energy and commodity resources, and strategic position spanning Central Asia and the Arctic.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: China is strategically incentivized to prevent a Russian collapse, implying limits on how far Beijing will let sanctions pressure weaken Moscow.
insights.quote: Beijing has reasons to keep Moscow strong enough to remain an independent power.
insights.locator: But it is missing an important aspect

insights.claim: Documented cases of Chinese material support to Russia's war economy include a Chinese state-owned firm shipping carbon fibre used in Geran attack drones to Alabuga-Volokno (a sanctioned Rosatom subsidiary, per Politico), Chinese engines and components found in Russian drones (Robert Lansing Institute), and Chinese drone specialists working with Russian manufacturers (Reuters).
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: Multiple independent reports point to a durable Chinese sanctions-evasion pipeline into Russia's drone supply chain; watch for targeted secondary sanctions on named Chinese state-owned suppliers.
insights.quote: a Chinese state-owned firm shipped carbon fibre used in Geran attack drones to Alabuga-Volokno, a sanctioned subsidiary of Rosatom
insights.locator: Documents reported this month by Politico

insights.claim: This evidence does not prove Beijing ordered every transaction or that Chinese support is 'limitless,' since Xi has no interest in becoming hostage to Putin's decisions and will keep calibrating China's exposure carefully.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: China's backing of Russia is opportunistic and bounded rather than unconditional, a key input for scenario planning on sanctions escalation.
insights.quote: Xi has no interest in becoming hostage to Putin’s decisions and Beijing will continue to calibrate its exposure very carefully
insights.locator: This does not prove that every transaction

insights.claim: For Beijing, Moscow functions as the 'useful disruptor-in-chief,' whose actions help an alternative multipolar international system emerge through groups like the SCO and BRICS in which US and European power carry less weight.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: China tolerates reputational cost from backing Russia because it advances Beijing's broader multipolarity project, not out of loyalty to Moscow.
insights.quote: For Beijing, Moscow remains the useful disruptor-in-chief.
insights.locator: For Beijing, Moscow remains the useful disruptor-in-chief

insights.claim: Europe's strategy of shaming governments into choosing between Russia and the West has clearly reached its limits, if not failed outright.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: EU diplomatic strategy premised on isolating Russia via pressure on third countries needs revision toward incentive-based engagement.
insights.quote: Their effort to shame governments into choosing between Russia and the West has clearly reached its limits – if not failed.
insights.locator: More realism is needed in Europe

insights.claim: The EU's approach to India, strengthening commercial ties while lowering its tone over New Delhi's relationship with Moscow, is offered as a better model for Europe's engagement with non-Western powers.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: A template to watch for replication with other Global South partners such as Kazakhstan and Central Asian states.
insights.quote: This has seen the EU strengthen commercial ties with India while lowering its tone over New Delhi’s relationship with Moscow.
insights.locator: The European Union (EU)’s relations with India

insights.claim: Europe can widen the space between Russia and its Asian partners by offering investment, technology, single-market access, critical-mineral partnerships, and alternative transport routes such as the Trans-Caspian corridor to reduce dependence on Russia.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: Flags concrete sectors, critical minerals, transport infrastructure, technology, where EU capital and policy could compete for regional influence against Russia and China.
insights.quote: Europe can offer investment, technology, access to the single market, and critical-mineral partnerships.
insights.locator: This makes sense: there is considerable scope

insights.claim: The EU has already sanctioned a growing number of Chinese companies involved in sanctions circumvention and Russia's military-industrial complex, and the success of Europe's long game hinges on how far it extends those sanctions to strategic supply chains involving larger or state-owned Chinese suppliers.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: Watch for EU sanctions expansion targeting Chinese state-owned firms tied to Russia's military supply chain as a policy catalyst.
insights.quote: the EU has already sanctioned a growing number of Chinese companies involved in sanctions circumvention and Russia’s military-industrial complex.
insights.locator: On China, the EU has already sanctioned

insights.claim: Putin's escalation shows he is wagering he can outlast Ukraine's Western supporters, believing Russia is sufficiently connected to the rest of the world to absorb Western pressure, and that his position is bolstered by a US he sees as weakened by its war with Iran.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: The durability of Western/Ukraine support and US bandwidth amid the Iran conflict are the key variables underpinning Putin's strategic bet.
insights.quote: he sees his position as bolstered by what he believes is a US weakened by war with Iran.
insights.locator: Russia’s escalation in Ukraine indicates

insights.claim: The author's central recommendation is that Europe must understand Putin's long-term strategic dynamics and respond with its own patient, long-game approach rather than expecting near-term Russian capitulation.
insights.speaker: Jon Wallace
insights.so_what: Sets expectations for a protracted conflict/standoff rather than near-term resolution, relevant for duration-based risk pricing in energy, defense spending, and sanctions regimes.
insights.quote: If Putin is playing the long game, perhaps it is time Europe does too.
insights.locator: closing line
